review:
I'm not going to say the game has zero merits, because honestly, there are some neat things about it. With that said, having been excited about this game and even having bought the Ultimate Edition, I can't recommend it to anyone. 

One of the main draws to this game for me, outside of simply seeing my favorite Shonen Jump characters together, was the character creator. Disappointingly, it's incredibly lackluster. Many of the clothes you can get in the game are just re-used from the characters that are already playable, and the rest are plain and generic. You can't customize the colors on them, either, which severely limits the creativity and control over your character's appearance. Similarly, your character's skills are limited only to those used by the in-game characters. While mixing and matching these can be interesting, the element system feels vestigial considering how few skills you can actually change the elements on. It's also rather disappointing that you can't apply them to other aspects of your character, such as their aura or hit graphics. It would've been nice to be able to choose more general fighting styles as well, although honestly, that makes little difference considering that every character in the game has the same attack strings, distinguished only by their varying skills. 

And that's something else about this game that drags it down. The characters I was looking forward to seeing in this game are absent entirely, replaced by mannequins wearing their faces. The story's writing is entirely devoid of any of the charm, depth, or nuance from the many series that it draws from. Every single character in the game has the same standing and talking animations. Their faces rarely animate outside of moving their mouths to talk. And they all speak in similar fashions, lacking their defining character traits outside of the most basic Shonen tropes that they share. (DOES ANYONE WANT SOME FOOD? HAHA THAT'S FUNNY RIGHT?)

Even all of those problems, I could have ignored if the gameplay were solid enough, but it's just not. While the basic movement is sound enough, it's unsatisfyingly difficult to chain combos into skills. Not only that, but the game punishes you for playing well; the Awakening meter, upon which every character relies to transform or perform Ultimate attacks, fills only when you take damage. While comeback mechanics are definitely a thing in many fighters and can work well, it is particularly egregious here because there is no way to acquire Awakening meter here other than getting wailed on. But even that isn't the worst of it; you would think that a comeback mechanic like this should require some skill to pull off successfully to make it not entirely unfair, right? Wrong. A lot of the time, it's incredibly easy to simply activate it while you're getting pummeled or when your enemy uses a skill of their own, leaving them absolutely no way to block it while in the middle of their own attack animation. This is, to put it simply, anti-competitive game design. 

To sum it up, the game lacks character, suffers from punishing skilled players / rewarding poor play, lacks diversity in character creation, and basically just feels like a generic third-rate game with beloved faces slapped on it. Don't buy this game. Appreciate it for what it could have been, and move on to something better before you waste your money.

Edit: A few afterthoughts. The game is set to Ultra graphics by default, and doesn't give you an options to change them until like almost half an hour into the game, which is the worst possible thing you could've done with those settings. Also, it crashes *all the time*. I kid you not, I booted it up earlier and took like two steps in the hub before it crashed on me. Not even exaggerating.

Sadly that's about the only 2 notable things about this game. So if you want to play anyone online you can either play your friends (which I recommend) or you can hop into quickmatch which will put you up against a sweaty tryhard 7/10 times. Last we have combos. You'd think there'd be deep combo depth with a game like this, but most people end up zoning/spamming abilities out of their butts like there's no tomorrow. Some characters like Aizen, Law, Zoro, Ichgio have good combo potential (there's a few more characters that probably haven't mentioned, but these are really the notable ones). Otherwise, most other characters in this game don't have much combo depth to them. If you can master combos, fighting other players will be quite a breeze (unless if they're spamming).

This player is usually pretty bad but will become the best player in the world all of a sudden.

Anyways enough about that rant, here comes the conclusion, should you buy the game? If it's on sale sure, otherwise it's not worth the full price. Play this game for fun, not worth trying to deal with this cancerous player base that's more toxic than the Call of Duty community.

In many ways, this game is just Dragonball Xenoverse with a different paint job, so I'll be writing this review of the game both taken on its own, and in comparison to Xenoverse.

[b]Anime Fan Appeal[/b]
This is the single biggest selling point of the game. If you're a big fan of Shounen anime, then this can be rather fun. There's a huge roster from across the Shonen Jump line-up, including characters from One Piece, Dragonball, Bleach, Naruto, Yu-gi-oh, Yuyu Hakusho, Saint Seiya, My Hero Academia, Hunter x Hunter, and more. In the "key missions" (story mode) there are a lot of interesting crossover pairings that allow for some amusing dialogue. This is the main point of the game, so it's good that it has some decent depth.

[b]Story[/b]
What story?

Okay, so there's a wafer-thin story here, but the vast majority of the missions, especially for the first 5 hours or so, are just recruitment. Go to location, see a little crossover banter, fight a character, done. There's something about a villain using a book to take people over using evil cubes, but that's mostly just an excuse to set up dozens of recruitment missions (and gives the impetus for most of the fights).

What's truly criminal, though, is that [b][i]there's no way to replay story missions[/i][/b]. To replay what little story there is, such as to watch the character interactions again or someone else in your family wants to play, you literally have to delete all your save game data - all characters, all progress, all everything. Even multiple characters are locked into the same story progress (even the same level, as I recall). This right here is one of the main reasons I had to give this game a negative review, like, some games have little replay value but this one [i]enforces[/i] zero replay value.

In comparison to Xenoverse, this game manages to have even less plot. The overall plot of Xenoverse is mostly just a paper-thin contrivance to let you relive the story of DBZ with a self-insert thrust into the story. Jump Force has an equally lacking plot, but doesn't even have an existing narrative to prop it up. It's just a paper-thin plot stringing together largely random fights. 

[b]Gameplay[/b]
The gameplay is mixed, but is mostly enjoyable. It's a solid 3D fighting game, with pretty simple button-mashing controls and lacks the more obtuse elements of a lot of "classic" fighting games (no wiggling the control stick in different directions to pull off 50 different moves). This means it has a much lower barrier to entry than games like Injustice, but in exchange fights can get a bit more repetitive as you'll be using the same combo a lot. 

My biggest complaint would be the stickiness of the controls. Buttons will sometimes work, but not at other times. A button sometimes won't trigger because of an animation that looks like it's over but actually still has a couple frames left. If often feels random whose super attack will activate first or penetrate the other - I've often pressed use on an ability only for the [i]enemy's[/i] ability to trigger, due to either a lag between pressing and activation, or the AI just veto'ing my ability use by using theirs instead.

Compared to Xenoverse, the control scheme is a bit different but the overall combat is very similar. Fights are always 1v1 in Jump Force, and always on the ground, so controls for flying and locking onto a target are removed. Also, not everyone has ki blasts. This lets core attacks like Grab have their own (controller) button instead of being a combo, a dedicated dash button, etc. 

Another feature is the party switch function that lets you switch between party members during a fight. All party members share the same health and ability bars, though personally, I'd like a pokemon-style switch where each party member has separate hp, and so you'd actually have to beat everyone on the opposing team individually. It still adds an interesting dynamic, and gives more tactical options.

Personally, I prefer the Jump Force controls over those of Xenoverse. It also helps that movesets and characters generally have a lot more variety in Jump Force. Regardless of race or playstyle in Xenoverse, you're going to have similar fights. Supers are a little different, and there's bias towards melee or ranged, but DBZ tends to have most of the fights be similar. 

Jump Force, in contrast, has fights that are incredibly different based on the character. I will actually put tactical thought into choosing my party, often prioritizing fast characters or characters with good reach or range, depending on the enemies. The difference between a non-fantasy sword master like Kenshin and a ranged specialist like Yusuke Urameshi can present a sizeable difference in playstyle, much more than "slightly biased towards melee or ranged supers" in Xenoverse.

[b]Overall[/b]
If you're a big anime fan, you'll probably enjoy this game. If you enjoyed Dragonball Xenoverse, and want something in the same vein but with more variety, you'll probably enjoy this game.

If you're not a big anime fan or easily get bored with button-mashers, this may not be the game for you. If you want a deep story with compelling characters like many of the anime featured in this game, you're also likely to be disappointed.

If you want a game you can replay and enjoy again, or if you want a game that multiple people can play through, definitely avoid this one.

I don't write many reviews so please bare with me as they tend to be ramblings lol. So the entirety of this games budgets was spent on the visuals. The special effects and stages are breathtaking to look at... Everything else... not so much. Some character models look fantastic, others... not so much especially with the mocap (cough, cough, dragon ball, cough). Also... they only animated the corners of Blackbeard's mouth, and anytime he has to speak it is terrifying. Aesthetics aside. Let's get into the gameplay.

So, if you've played Xenoverse or the Ninja Storm games, you'll be familiar with how this game plays. It takes aspects of both... and fails miserably... The tag mechanics are a little different, whereas in Ninja Storm, your allies would be attached to a bumper, only your 1st ally is attached to Left Trigger, meaning if you want to use the next assist, you have to tag through to the next character. Also, if you want to tag to the next character, you tap the trigger, and hold for an assist. Not terrible, but at times it feels like my assists aren't working as I'm accidentally tagging in. The last issue with tagging for me, is that the cooldown is obscenely short for assists. You can spam the absolute hell out of your assist.

The BIGGEST issue for me overall is blocking. I'm noticing that you can sit there and block for an eternity if the first attack IS NOT a guard break. You can block absolutely everything with very little penalty at times. For example, I TRIED using spirit bomb as my super, and it was ALWAYS blocked, and did barely any chip damage. If you're on the offensive, and the opponent is blocking, the moment your combo stops to attempt a guard break or throw (btw... throws are painful. I literally watch my character gently brush my opponents hair and nothing happens) the enemy can counter attack with their own combo or spam a super move since everything stops to display their animation. This makes AI battles in story very frustrating... worse so in online.

I've got almost 10 hours in this... really wish I stopped at 2 so I could get the refund and be done with this but I tried anyways. Online matches for me have been as follows. If the connection is good, I use Piccolo's Special Beam Cannon assist and start a combo. Before the combo even ends, Special Beam Cannon is ready to fire again. Rinse and repeat. If the connection is bad, your painful watching as your character stutters across the screen flailing madly as the opponent blocks. Mid combo, they use Kaguya's Vacuum fist and pulverize you. Assists and supers in this game are so easy to exploit that there is no substance at all the combat at all. Again, all of this is from MY experience, others may disagree. But after 2 days of playing with only 2 losses. I think I have a pretty good idea about how I feel about this game.

Overall:
Pros:
Take some of my absolute FAVORITE characters from multiple franchises and pit them against one another. Its a HUGE roster and I'm super pleased with the variety. Could be some more female characters as only Boa and Kaguya are in the roster but thats nit picking.

Visually the game looks amazing. The moves are cinematic, flashy and over the top. Exactly like the animes they represent.
The stages are vibrant and exciting to look at. A lot of imagination went into mashing these worlds together and I think they nailed it.

Cons:
Jesus christ the mocap on the dragon ball characters looks ridiculous. Outside of combat they look SO out of place and its jarring as all hell. Also... the TEETH. I dont know why, but they look so out of place... Speaking of teeth... BLACKBEARD is horrifying to look at.

Combat has absolutely no substance whatsoever. Use a super to interrupt literally anything. The amount of wake up finisher attacks I've landed and been hit with... Certain super attacks and assists are overpowered and can be exploited for easy wins, so why bother using anything else? Blocking is busted as well. Overall the combat is bland and very lack luster.

Netcode is... ok. It's either perfect or just garbage. There is no middle ground.

Overall, the only thing this game has going for it is the visuals. Outside of that, not much else. I'll give it a 3/10 tops, which is  a shame, I wanted to like this game very much. If you're a fan of these series and love "worlds collide" scenarios, maybe you'll enjoy it more than I did.

The number of characters is nice, there are 58 including the custom character and they all have different timing, technique and movements, which leaves a great diversity of gameplay even if some characters are very little played and it's a pity, they are all strong when you master them well. The clan system is nice but only useful during certain events. The customization of your character is relatively bad, you can't do much body modification and you can't change the color of your clothes, which leaves little freedom if you want to create a particular character. I hear a lot of people say that there are no more players in PvP, personally I find a game in 5 to 30 seconds in quick match, in ranked it takes more time because if you want to level up from rank B, you find less players. The ranking system is very punitive because if we fall on an opponent who has 5+ level less than us and we win, we get only 1 point while if we lose it's about 200/250 points less while knowing that there are 500 points between each rank. It can happen that there are some bugs but there are few and those of jump force remain minimal. To summarize, we could say that all the budget of the game has been put in the fights and the characters and that the rest has been neglected

Disadvantages:

- Very limited customization
- Boring story mode

Advantages:

- Technical and epic fights
- Nice graphic effects (but not exceptional)

The game is fun with friends, learning the mechanics is a thrill, and gameplay is good based on personal perspective but:

TL;DR - Despite a staggering number of flaws, Jump Force is a lot of fun to play.

Note: Game is being removed from Steam February 8, 2022.

Jump Force has only one good aspect: the gameplay. It's what is sometimes called a "3D arena fighter". Which basically means you move fast and have a large combat area. Played any of the Ultimate Ninja Storm games? Then you've played this. Jump Force has only minor differences.

It's far easier than most fighting games. There's no need to memorize long and difficult combos. You just mash the attack button. Dodges require more finesse. Overall, even a young child could play this.

Jump Force follows the "easy to learn hard to master" philosophy of game design. There's a bit of depth beyond the simplicity. Choosing the right time to dodge is tricky. Some special (super?) moves can be cancelled into from regular attacks. However, they don't always connect. Timing is critical, but not so strict that you'll want to throw the controller in frustration.

No opponent (so far) as been undefeatable. The difficulty lowers with every rematch. Keep trying, and you'll eventually get it. Even if you are really bad at fighting games. (Like me.)

The playable characters include many of the most popular anime/manga characters of all time. Goku, Ichigo, Naruto, Yusuke, Luffy, and more. Many are from series I've never seen. On the surface, this seems really cool. The problem is that the character designs don't mesh. 

There's been an attempt to give them all a "realistic" appearance. At the same time, a lot of the hair looks like plastic. Just like an action figure. It's painfully obvious that they are anime characters in the real world. Maybe that's what they were going for? I don't know. It's really weird, though. 

I mean, Luffy's mouth has got to be 9 inches wide. With larger (and more) teeth than any human being has ever had. At the same time, he has highly realistic rippling abs. I don't know if it's the uncanny valley, but it's definitely close.

You're required to have a custom character to play through the story. The customization options are very limiting. The male character looks like a half-Japanese twink. I can't get him to look any different than that. You can't have huge muscles. You can't be fat, bald, old, bearded, or ugly. You can't have big lips, a sloping brow, beady eyes, or a crooked nose. I wanted a Kuwabara-type character. So, I found this disappointing.

The default costume choices are awful. Literally just the clothes of other characters in Jump Force. Once you get into the game, you can obtain more. These are largely re-colors, and rather generic. You can really only look like a cosplayer or a nerd.

Jump Force makes the bold choice of having the protagonist be silent. It's just... weird. Characters talk to me like Timmy talks to Lassie. They give me commands, tell me what they are doing, or guess at my thoughts. That's the limit of our interactions. My character doesn't even nod.

I was given one dialog option. Which seems to have been completely irrelevant. No impact on the game at all. (As far as I can tell.)

Oh, and the dialog is in Japanese. There's no spoken English. It's just subtitles. Many of the missions have no spoken dialog at all. It's just text. While the characters stare at one another with blank expressions and closed mouths. However, some characters have mouth movement during these moments. Which makes it seem like the game is partially unfinished.

There's barely any story. None of which is good. The characters are all pulled to the "real world" from their respective realities. The good guys all team-up. They proceed to beat-up venoms. People infected with [i]something[/i] that makes them evil. 

After beating up other heroes, they remove the venom. At which point the hero joins them without resistance. For some reason, the heroes require me to remove it. But all I do is stare at them while a droid does it. I don't control the robot. I don't understand why my character needs to be there.

In the text, other characters reference me specifically, by name. Yet they never say my name. It's strange.

The characters aren't well-written. In fact, they often act in ways that run counter to their personalities. Yusuke teams up without a thought. Even though he's a distrusting loner with a bad attitude. Ichigo wants to chase down an enemy, but he's asked not to. So, he complies. Despite being a person that does whatever his anger compels him to do. Even if that means lying, breaking promises, risking his life, or even the lives of others.

Between fights, you'll be taken back to a hub world. It serves the same function as a menu. Only it takes 60+ seconds to run to the person you need to talk to continue the game. Rather than highlighting a selection and pushing a button.

The hub world's only purpose is to show off player avatars to each other. But they all look silly or lame. So, who cares? I suppose it breaks up the tedium of match-after-match of fights.

There's even this giant ring around the hub. It takes about 4.5 minutes to run all the way around it. It's empty. Except for a single NPC that endlessly runs laps... in a business suit. Why is this here? Your guess is as good as mine.

The game progresses by taking on missions. Most are accepted from one of several mission counters. Others require you to talk to an NPC. Regardless, each starts with dry dialog. One to three battles follow. Then you get a bit more dry dialog.

There's an xp and leveling system. You'll sometimes find battles get too difficult. You can gain levels by playing "free missions" repeatedly.

And that's Jump Force! While it isn't a great game, it's fun.

This game is confusing, it's a poor execution of a style of anime fighting game that's been done beautifully many times before. I've gotten everything out of this game that I can and that's just sad. 6.6 hours including the time it's taken me to leave and come back after getting bored and watching an episode of something on netflix. I love the idea of taking these beloved characters and pitting them against any and everybody and their grandmother, but this was just lazy. The graphics are fine after adjusting, but it loses me when the characters are ham-fisted into this forced rationalization for their gathering. The glaring offense, however, is the gameplay. I have NEVER been so bored in a fighting game after so short a time. It's not too formulaic or simplistic, rather it feels random, you get punished for taking the right path sometimes. I'm no savant in fighting games but I can usually identify structure and try to play by the rules. You would do better in this game as someone who knows nothing about video games at all than someone trying to understand the mechanics and improve. The balance is way off, and there's a general lack of depth to anything that you do. It's less about skill, and more about landing a basic combo that does ludicrous damage. The worst is the lack of surprise. Normally, a game structured like this would be frustrating, but everything else in the game almost lets you know what to expect ahead of time. The character creation is . . . present by the loosest definition. The best way to explain is that I played very little of the game as my custom character. The only reason to do so is to try and grab some of the cheap moves and put them all on one guy to be better online. This is a system that comes straight from genre, but let me know it was lazily done. I love the Xenoverse games, the system of taking moves from other characters makes more sense when it's consistent. In Xenoverse, you get to make the moves your own almost, any attack is a technique with obvious tradeoff, and you end up with a wide set of playstyles that can be viably used. Here, you know exactly whose moves someone is using, where they came from and the reason is because they're specific to a limited roster. There's only as much variety as there are characters. Here, that just takes away from the characters. It feels like someone trying to build their ideal body by cutting various limbs from pictures in a bunch of magazines, resulting in a hideously malformed collage of vain insecurity. The bottom line is that this game is lazy. It can be inoffensive for a little under an hour, but if you stop staring at the explosions and exaggerated physics for too long, and start thinking of the potential changes that would've made it truly enjoyable it's heartbreaking. I'm not mad, just disappointed.

The combat is just as tedious, and I think it's just as unfinished as the rest of the game. The special move mechanic is so awful that once you get someone's special meter to 50% it's just turtling up until they attempt to fire at you so you can block it, and if you do anything that locks you into an animation, you'll be hit by their ultimate the moment they fire it because they're literally all instant and have hyper armor. Added on top of this, you don't gain meter from actually doing well, you only get meter if you get hit, so it's incentivizing defensive play to the point where it's just gotten boring. Every single match I fight goes like this: I beat them up, they get their ultimate, they use their ultimate. If it hits me, it charges my meter up enough that I hit them ONE time because any basic attack in the game assures my ultimate move hits, then I use mine. The fight ends. Repeat. If it doesn't hit me, I just continue beating them up until they do it again. The game isn't fleshed out, it's tedious in every single way, making money is awful, getting gear is awful, fighting is awful, customization is awful. On a bright note the fighting does LOOK wonderful. It's a very pretty game in terms of attack animations, but that's the only good thing I can really say about it if I'm honest.

Starting off this review I have to point out that I’m a massive Dragon Ball fan, I don’t really take an interest in any of the other Animes, but I have a bias towards anything Dragon Ball. When this game was first shown at E3, I was hyped beyond belief. Showing Namek, Goku and Frieza with the art style taken had blown me away, I was sold on the game before gameplay had even come out. That’s the power of hype though folks and I’ve been proven wrong plenty of times before and I never learn my lesson.

I pre-ordered the Deluxe edition of the game at around £75 but I haven’t made a massive game purchase this year so I thought I could splurge my money on this one. I did have some mixed feelings about spending that much, but I thought it would be worth it. The £50 price is the base price. I’ll start with the positive aspects of the game and move on to the negatives later.

The game has a massive roster that would definitely please more hardcore Anime/Manga fans, Dragon Ball, Naruto, One Piece, Bleach, the list goes on and on. With the character pass there is an obvious intent to add a lot more characters later on and keep working on this game as time goes on, as long as it doesn’t completely flop.

The fighting can be slightly tedious, but I quite liked the movesets and combos. Launching a big bang attack in this game truly did feel badass, along with many of the other signature ultimate moves that come with this game.

Now I’m going to dive into the negative side of the review. I refunded this game before I fell into a sunk cost fallacy because I knew that would happen to me eventually. I wanted to love this game from the very start, I wanted to be hyped and watch these different anime characters battling it out with original characters from Akira Toriyama himself.

I did not love this game, I didn’t even like it and I regretted it after about an hour of play. The mission system is very similar to Xenoverse but worse, it’s tedious and void of actual content. The actual story is lacklustre and really pointless, the whole story is centred around fighting different anime characters and generic evil beings that can take power and control other people which isn’t exciting at all and no different from completing the side missions or just doing your own fight.

The art style is another thing to comment on with this game, when I look at Goku it’s almost like someone spray painted a Goku face onto a WWE custom character. It’s off-putting to say the least, considering the trailer actually looked really good the game doesn’t live up to it. I didn’t have fun with this game either, it just felt like I was going through chores rather than watching the most popular anime characters fight.

The final negative point I have to make about this game may be a controversial one, it’s just a personal preference which may be the same for some others too. I did not enjoy any of the voice acting, I prefer watching dub in anime rather than sub and it put me off that there wasn’t a choice. I was well aware before purchasing but I didn’t realise I’d dislike it that much, I’m also well aware that they couldn’t really do anything about this due to the fact that licensing all the different characters in the game is pretty much an impossible task due to multiple rights holders.

In conclusion, I should’ve enjoyed this game, I should be defending it due to my bias but unfortunately, I cannot recommend this at all. Maybe I have been a bit harsh and been let down by the standards I gave the game after the trailer, but I genuinely don’t think it’s worth it. I may revisit this when it’s around about £5-10. I’d rate this 3 disappointing E3s out of 12.
